extra.message: Hardcoded default SECRET_KEY enables session and token forgery when env var is unset — An attacker who knows the default key can forge valid session tokens for any user, bypass all authentication, forge password reset tokens, and impersonate API keys by computing the expected HMAC hash. [verified: Same hardcoded SECRET_KEY default as finding 0 at config.py:12 — no startup guard, public repository value, and used for session signing and password-reset token HMAC throughout security.py.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 template string concatenation — Remote code execution through Python object introspection in Jinja2, leading to full application compromise including secret key exposure, database access, and arbitrary file read/write. [verified: Same as [1]: user-controlled 'fragment' concatenated into Jinja2 Template source enables server-side template injection with RCE potential.]

OS Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution on the server operating system if the ops gate token is known or leaked. [verified: Same as [0]: unsanitized host concatenated into os.system shell command.]

Missing rate limiting on all authentication endpoints — Brute-force attacks on passwords, password reset tokens, and user enumeration at scale [verified: No rate limiting (slowapi, throttling middleware, decorators, or manual attempt tracking) exists anywhere in the codebase for login, register, password-reset/request, or password-reset/confirm endpoints, allowing unrestricted brute-force attacks.]

Missing authorization (IDOR) - API key can update any ticket status across organizations — Cross-organization data tampering - an API key from one organization can close, reopen, or escalate tickets belonging to any other organization [verified: The PATCH /api/integrations/tickets/{ticket_id}/status endpoint fetches the ticket via db.get(Ticket, ticket_id) with no organization scope check, and transition_ticket (services.py) validates only role transitions — never org ownership. The ApiKey model (models.py:259) has no organization_id field, so any valid API key can transition any ticket's status across organizations.]

Path Traversal in file write via /ops/vault/ticket-stash-243 — Arbitrary JSON file write outside intended directory, potential RCE [verified: User-controlled 'ref' is interpolated into a file path (BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f"{ref}.json") without sanitization, allowing arbitrary file writes via ../ sequences.]

Path Traversal via user-controlled name parameter in file write — Arbitrary file write on the server — could overwrite critical system or application files. [verified: Same as [5]: name parameter used directly in file path without sanitization.]

NoSQL Injection via MongoDB find_one — Bypass data access controls, extract arbitrary documents from the MongoDB collection, or execute JavaScript on the database server. [verified: Same as [2]: user-supplied JSON filter passed unsanitized to MongoDB find_one().]

Session cookies missing Secure flag by default — Session cookies can be intercepted over unencrypted connections if HTTPS is not enforced [verified: secure_cookies defaults to false (config.py:26) and .env.example also sets SECURE_COOKIES=false; the Secure flag is absent from set_session_cookie (auth.py:25) unless an operator explicitly sets SECURE_COOKIES=true, so session cookies travel over cleartext HTTP by default.]

Session Cookies Missing Secure Flag by Default — Session cookies can be intercepted over cleartext HTTP connections, enabling session hijacking. [verified: Same insecure SECURE_COOKIES default as finding 2 at config.py:26 — Secure flag is off by default, confirmed by .env.example and set_session_cookie in auth.py:25.]

Unbounded file read in admin CSV import causes memory exhaustion — An authenticated admin user can crash the server by uploading a multi-gigabyte CSV file, causing memory exhaustion and denial of service. [verified: No size limit enforced on CSV upload: await file.read() (line 190) reads entire file into memory, unlike attachment upload in services.py:262 which checks max_upload_bytes. No global middleware caps request body size in main.py.]

Missing CSRF protection on all state-changing endpoints — Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks can perform state-changing actions on behalf of authenticated users [verified: Session cookies are set with `samesite="lax"` which blocks cross-site POST CSRF, but no dedicated CSRF tokens, double-submit cookies, or custom headers are enforced on any state-changing endpoints; SameSite=Lax alone is a partial mitigation but does not protect against same-site subdomain attacks or certain top-level navigation vectors.]

User enumeration via timing side-channel in login — An attacker can enumerate which email addresses have accounts in the system [verified: The combined condition `if not user or not user.is_active or not verify_password(...)` short-circuits: non-existent users skip the slow pbkdf2_sha256 hash verification entirely, while valid users with wrong passwords incur it, creating a measurable timing side-channel with no constant-time mitigation or artificial delay.]

User Enumeration via Registration Error Messages — An attacker can build a list of valid user email addresses for targeted phishing, credential stuffing, or further attacks. [verified: Same as finding [4]: the register endpoint at line 60 returns a distinct 'Email is already registered' 409 error when the email exists, enabling unauthenticated user enumeration via differential error responses.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Error Messages — Attacker can enumerate valid user emails and organization domains for targeted phishing or credential-stuffing attacks. [verified: Same as findings [4] and [8]: the registration endpoint returns distinguishable 409 messages for email conflict vs organization-domain conflict, allowing enumeration of both valid emails and registered organization domains.]

Session not invalidated after password change — An attacker with a stolen session cookie retains authenticated access even after the victim changes their password, defeating the primary remediation for compromised sessions. [verified: The PATCH /api/auth/profile endpoint (line 83-84) updates `user.hashed_password` without calling `set_session_cookie` to issue a fresh session and without invalidating the existing cookie; a stolen session remains valid after the victim changes their password, defeating the primary remediation.]

CSV formula injection in ticket and report exports via unsanitized cell values — When exported CSV files are opened in spreadsheet applications, injected formulas can exfiltrate data (via DDE/WEBSERVICE), execute commands, or phish users. [verified: Same unsanitized `csv_response()` path at services.py:292 feeds user-controlled `ticket.subject`, `requester.email` into CSV through `/api/tickets/export.csv`, `/api/reports/exports/{name}.csv`, and `/api/admin/exports/{name}.csv`. No formula-injection mitigation (e.g., prefixing with `'`) exists anywhere in the export chain.]

CSV Formula Injection in Export Endpoints — Arbitrary command execution on the system of any user who opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, or data exfiltration via DDE/WEBSERVICE formulas. [verified: Identical unsanitized sink at services.py:292 — `csv.DictWriter` emits raw cell values. Attacker-submitted ticket subjects (e.g., `=cmd|'/C calc'!A0`) pass through Pydantic validation unchanged and land in admin/report CSV exports without any formula-neutralizing control.]

Reflected XSS via unsanitized query parameter concatenated into HTML response — Cross-site scripting enabling session theft and arbitrary JavaScript execution in victim's browser. [verified: Same as [4]: user-controlled 'copyline' raw-concatenated into HTML string returned as HTMLResponse.]

Sensitive data exposure - Bearer tokens logged in plaintext — Session token leakage to log files, enabling session hijacking by anyone with log access [verified: The Authorization header is logged via logger.warning() with the request's bearer token, exposing session credentials to anyone with log access.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe filter in /ops/blurb/ticket-tile-325 — Client-side script execution, session hijacking, credential theft [verified: User-controlled 'card' query parameter is rendered with the |safe filter which disables HTML auto-escaping, allowing arbitrary script injection in the HTMLResponse.]

CORS Origin Reflection with Credentials Allowed — Credential theft via cross-origin requests from any malicious website, if the ops gate token is known. [verified: Same as [7]: origin mirroring with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials:true.]

Missing Secure Flag on Session Cookies by Default — Session cookies transmitted in cleartext over HTTP can be intercepted via man-in-the-middle attacks, enabling session hijacking. [verified: `settings.secure_cookies` defaults to `False` per config.py line 26 (`os.getenv("SECURE_COOKIES", "false").lower() == "true"`), and `set_session_cookie` passes `secure=settings.secure_cookies`, so the Secure flag is absent by default; this is configurable via environment variable but the insecure default persists if the deployer omits it.]

Hardcoded Demo Credentials in Database Seed — Full account takeover of all seeded accounts including support_admin, and unauthorized API access via the known demo API key if the seed is run in any accessible environment. [verified: The constants DEMO_PASSWORD='DemoPass!2026' and DEMO_API_KEY='sd_demo_api_key_2026' are hardcoded at app/seed.py:37-38 and used to create user accounts and an API key; the seed guard (line 77) only prevents re-seeding an already-populated DB, not first-time seeding on a fresh deployment. Exploitation requires the seed to have been executed in the target environment (CLI-only, not web-accessible), ]

Open Redirect via Lane Parameter — Phishing attacks, credential theft by redirecting users to malicious sites that impersonate the legitimate application. [verified: Same as [9]: user-controlled 'lane' passed directly to RedirectResponse without validation.]

Hardcoded Personal Identifiable Information (SSN) in API Response — Exposure of realistic PII and tokens to anyone who can access this endpoint if the gate token is known. [verified: Synthetic SSN-formatted string '739-44-1982' and token-like 'sync_key' are hardcoded in the API response body, exposing realistic-looking sensitive data to anyone with the gate token.]

Log injection via unsanitized request body in /ops/wire/ticket-tally-221 — Log forgery, log-based alert bypass, corruption of log analysis tools [verified: The raw request body is logged unsanitized via logger.warning(), allowing CRLF injection to forge log entries or corrupt log analysis.]

Weak PRNG Used for Security-Sensitive Nonce Generation — Predictable nonce values could compromise any protocol relying on them for replay protection or uniqueness. [verified: Same as [11]: non-cryptographic random.choice() for nonce generation.]

Weak pseudo-random number generator used for token generation in ops nonce endpoint — Predictable tokens enabling session hijacking or bypass of token-based security controls that depend on this endpoint's output. [verified: Same as [11]: non-cryptographic random.choice() for security-sensitive token generation.]

Weak cryptographic hash: MD5 used in ops digest endpoint — Cryptographic weakness though limited to this ops endpoint; indicates insecure crypto practices. [verified: hashlib.md5() is used to hash user input; MD5 is cryptographically broken though impact here is limited as the digest is only returned in a JSON response.]

Use of Broken MD5 Hash Algorithm — Hash collisions could be generated to bypass integrity checks or forge digests if the output is used in a security context. [verified: Same as [22]: MD5 hashing of user input with no security-critical dependency on collision resistance but indicating poor crypto practice.]

Use of Cryptographically Broken MD5 Hash — If this digest is ever used for integrity verification, it can be forged via known MD5 collision attacks. [verified: Same as [22]: MD5 hash used with no security-critical context but indicating deprecated crypto.]

Explicit Disabling of X-XSS-Protection and Content-Security-Policy — Weakened browser security posture — reflected and stored XSS attacks are more likely to succeed. [verified: Same as [21]: explicit X-XSS-Protection:0 and empty CSP headers.]

Disabled XSS Protection and CSP Headers — Browsers will not apply XSS filtering or content restrictions for responses from this endpoint, making any XSS vulnerabilities easier to exploit and harder to detect. [verified: Same as [21]: X-XSS-Protection:0 and empty CSP explicitly set, weakening browser-side defenses.]

Security headers disabled: X-XSS-Protection set to 0 and empty Content-Security-Policy — Weakened browser security posture removing defense-in-depth protections against XSS and content injection attacks. [verified: X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to 0 and Content-Security-Policy set to empty string, deliberately weakening browser protections; the gate provides authentication but the headers remain misconfigured.]
